Introduction

More than right and wrong.

“What do these values actually look like in everyday life?”

This portfolio brings together ten moral reflections, our Gen Z project from GERE 210 and the documentary my friend and I produced at Matbakh Maryam. I wanted to record what I remember from this semester, from debates and activities to our group presentation, rather than simply repeat what was written in the lectures.

My moral views have generally aligned with the Catholic Church, and our professor usually expressed a similar perspective. Some conversations, especially IVF, reminded me that knowing real people facing a difficult situation can make it harder to give a simple answer. Listening to different opinions helped me understand why these questions matter.

What links the topics for me is the dignity of every human person. As a computer engineering student, I also see how the choices I make, the people I work with and the technology I create can reflect these values.

Closing reflection

What I’m taking with me.

Values become meaningful when we put them into practice.

Looking back, what I remember most is not just the definitions, but the conversations: the debate about burkinis, the picture of the little girl painting, the story about abuse, the group presentation, our Gen Z project and the videos on difficult questions about human life. They made the course feel connected to the world we live in. My faith continues to shape my moral beliefs, and these discussions reminded me to listen respectfully to people whose experiences are different from mine.

Our documentary at Matbakh Maryam brought those values into practice. It showed how solidarity and the preferential option for the poor can become part of everyday life. I hope to carry this sense of responsibility into my own life and future work.
